archetype.name: Improviser (with new short-area precision)
archetype.definition: A third-year quarterback who still holds the ball, extends plays and scrambles for value, but now pairs that with the most accurate underneath passing of his career.

report.headline: The accuracy leap is real; the intermediate turnovers are the bill still coming due
report.take:
Caleb Williams has always been a creator who holds the ball. His time to throw is 3.19 this year, against 3.20 last year, and he still escapes to scramble on about one dropback in thirteen. What has changed is everything after the ball leaves his hand. In his first two seasons his bad-throw rate ranked 53rd and 52nd at the position. This year it is 9.7%, fourth-best of 42. His completion rate is up 10.6 points on last season, and his CPOE has swung 9.7 points. That is not a hot week. It is a different passer through six starts, and it fits a second year under Ben Johnson: 7.61 intended air yards, a negative air-yards-to-sticks figure and a lower aggressiveness rate all point to a quarterback taking what the structure gives him.

The engine is the short game. On throws of 0-9 air yards he completes 80.2% with a 9.4 CPOE, and those 86 attempts produce the largest EPA total of any depth band. Rome Odunze supplies the explosive layer on top of it: 0.922 EPA per target on 28 looks, a figure no one else in the room comes close to. Williams' 0.198 EPA per dropback ranks 10th of 49. His sack rate sits below the league average even though his pressure-to-sack rate has slipped, because the scrambles, at 0.706 EPA each with nine first downs on 18 runs, pay back much of what the hold-the-ball style costs.

The numbers flatter him in one way and hide a flaw in another. The flattery comes from Week 1, an 18.6-EPA blowout at Carolina that still props up the season averages. His last three games run at 0.122 EPA per dropback, good but not top-ten good. The hidden flaw is the 10-19 yard window. He completes just 45.8% there with a negative CPOE and three of his five interceptions, and his game state with a 9-plus-point lead carries a -0.229 EPA per play with three picks. Week 9's four-interception night against Tampa Bay, the league's second-best defense by EPA today, was the loudest version of a real pattern, not a one-off.

Where it heads: the accuracy gains look structural, and the sack and scramble trade is a fair one. The interception rate is the swing variable. His career says he has usually been a low-turnover passer, so some of the recent spike should cool. The intermediate inaccuracy is also new, though, and needs watching. Expect a top-12-ish efficiency passer who wins with volume underneath rather than a weekly ceiling game.

strengths.title: Short-area accuracy, transformed
strengths.body: Underneath, he is now close to automatic, with an 80.2% completion rate and a 9.4 CPOE on 0-9 yard throws. His overall bad-throw rate has dropped from the bottom of the league to fourth-best. Because his time to throw has not changed, this reads as cleaner mechanics and better structure rather than a quicker game, which makes it the most sustainable part of his season.

strengths.title: Scrambles pay for the hold
strengths.body: He still extends plays, and when he breaks the pocket it is a strong play: 0.706 EPA per scramble, with half of his scrambles moving the chains. That is why a 3.19-second time to throw coexists with a sack rate below the league average. It has been a career trait, with his rushing yards ranking 7th in both prior seasons, so it should hold.

strengths.title: Red-zone precision
strengths.body: Inside the 20 he has five touchdowns, no interceptions and a 12.0 CPOE on 26 attempts. His overall TD rate ranks only 28th, which partly reflects two rushing scores and a low-aggression approach. With this red-zone efficiency, the touchdown pace has room to rise rather than fall, though the sample is small.

concerns.title: Intermediate window produces the turnovers
concerns.body: On 10-19 yard throws he completes 45.8% with a negative CPOE and three interceptions on 48 attempts. That is the one depth where the accuracy leap has not shown up. The EPA there is still positive because the completions are big, but this is where drives die. It is a genuine flaw to fix, not a cost of the style.

concerns.title: Interceptions rising lately
concerns.body: His last-three-game interception rate is 3.8%, driven by four picks against Tampa Bay's top-two defense. He has also been loose when protecting big leads, at -0.229 EPA per play with three interceptions when up 9-plus. His career ints ranked mid-pack, so some cooling is likely, but the trend points the wrong way.

concerns.title: Pressure turning into sacks again
concerns.body: His pressure-to-sack rate is 29.5%, ranking 24th of 42, far off last year's 15.9%, which ranked 4th. Holding the ball has always carried this risk. The left tackle, Braxton Jones, is now out for the season, so the protection that kept this in check is thinner.

trend.note: After the Week 1 explosion and a Week 2 dud against Minnesota's top-ranked defense, he strung together three efficient games from Weeks 6 to 8, then piled up yards but gave the ball away four times against Tampa Bay. Yardage has ticked up lately, while efficiency has settled below the season figure that Week 1 inflates.

nextGame.headline: Saints' leaky secondary sets up well after the bye
nextGame.body:
New Orleans ranks 22nd in pass defense EPA and dead last in deep-pass EPA. It allows 274.6 passing yards a game to quarterbacks, 29th in the league, and gives up explosive passes at the 27th-worst rate. That suits both halves of his game. The underneath volume should flow against a defense that is 22nd on short passes, and Odunze's downfield efficiency meets the softest deep defense in the league. The Saints do generate sacks, ranking 7th in sack rate, so his long time to throw and recent pressure-to-sack slippage are the one real risk. Opposing WR1s and lead tight ends have both found room against them.

Availability matters on both sides. Luther Burden III, tied for the team lead in targets, is questionable with a concussion. If he sits, more volume shifts to Odunze, Colston Loveland and Kalif Raymond. Braxton Jones is already gone for the year, which leaves the edge protection a question against a pass rush that gets home. On the Saints' side, the offense ranks 22nd in EPA and is missing Travis Etienne Jr., CJ Donaldson and center Erik McCoy. That raises the odds Chicago plays from ahead, a game state where Williams has been careless this year. No line is posted yet, and the Bears come off 14 days of rest.

keyMatchups.title: Odunze against the league's worst deep defense
keyMatchups.body: Odunze has been the offense's explosive play-maker per target, and New Orleans allows more EPA on deep throws than anyone. With Burden questionable, this is where the ceiling of the game lives.

keyMatchups.title: Saints pass rush against thin protection
keyMatchups.body: New Orleans ranks 7th in sack rate, and Williams is converting pressure to sacks far more than last year with his left tackle out. His scrambles are the counter if he gets clean escape lanes.

keyMatchups.title: Loveland against a soft TE coverage
keyMatchups.body: The Saints rank 28th in EPA allowed per target to lead tight ends. Loveland already carries a top-two share of the targets, and he becomes even more central if Burden is out.

nextGame.watch: Whether the intermediate throws stay clean once Chicago builds a lead, since that is where his interceptions have come from.

restOfSeason.body:
The accuracy gains underneath and the scramble value have the profile of real, lasting changes: they come with an unchanged time to throw and a career-long rushing trait, and they held up across good and bad opponents. Expect roughly 245-280 passing yards a game with a completion rate in the high 60s. His touchdown output should edge up toward 1.3-1.8 a game given his red-zone precision. The efficiency will likely sit below the Week 1-inflated season figure, closer to what he has done since.

The interception rate is the thing most likely to move. The intermediate inaccuracy and late-lead sloppiness are real, but four picks in one game against an elite defense overstate the problem, and his history says 0.5-0.9 a game is more typical. Sacks are the other drag. With the left tackle gone and a 3.19-second clock, two-plus a game is the baseline, and the scrambles have to keep paying for them.
swingFactors: Odunze's health and Burden's return from concussion

confidence.note: Six starts, one outlier opener; accuracy change is large and consistent but young.
